subject: philosophy
title: Knowledge and ignorance
objective: Learn why recognizing a limit differs from denying all knowledge.

lesson.opening: TEXTUAL CONTEXT: In Apology 21b–23b, Socrates describes examining people reputed wise. The familiar slogan “I know that I know nothing” is not the sentence quoted here. Read the actual contrast in Plato’s portrayal.

sections.heading: Confidence proportioned to grounds
sections.body:
The contrast is between lacking a kind of knowledge while claiming it and lacking it without that pretense. The passage need not be read as a formal proof that Socrates has no knowledge whatsoever. It identifies an advantage concerning awareness of a limit.

Later in the speech, Socrates acknowledges the artisans’ genuine expertise while criticizing their extension of that expertise to matters beyond it. A skilled builder may know how to build without thereby knowing every answer about justice. Respect for expertise and criticism of overreach can coexist.

Intellectual humility is not the habit of adding “maybe” to every statement. It concerns how your confidence relates to your grounds, your ability to explain those grounds, and your willingness to revise. Excessive doubt can be as poorly calibrated as excessive certainty.

INTERPRETIVE LIMIT: The scope of Socratic professions of ignorance and their relation to his moral commitments are debated. Avoid turning a particular passage into a slogan that erases other claims in the speech.

sections.heading: Reconstructing the argument
sections.body: The advantage is limited: the speaker does not add a false claim of knowledge to ignorance. This does not entail that he possesses a complete account of virtue, nor that all genuine expertise is impossible.

sections.heading: A serious objection
sections.body: A critic asks whether a person who confidently says another lacks knowledge must himself possess standards of knowledge. A thoughtful interpretation must examine those standards rather than treating ignorance as a self-explanatory virtue.

activities.prompt: What advantage is claimed in this passage?
choices: Not thinking he knows what he does not know.
Having no need to examine himself.

activities.prompt: Why does acknowledging artisans’ expertise matter?
choices: It blocks the inference that the speech simply denies all human knowledge.
It proves artisans know every moral truth.

activities.prompt: An excellent engineer gives an unsupported view about a historical event. What should you do?
choices: Accept it because expertise transfers to every subject.
Assess the relevant historical evidence while respecting the engineering expertise.

activities.prompt: Which question targets the critic’s concern?
choices: What standards justify the claim that another person lacks knowledge?
The passage contrasts pretense with recognition of ignorance.
The passage proves Socrates denies every possible item of knowledge.
Calibrating confidence to grounds and acknowledging limits.

activities.prompt: Describe a subject you know something about. Identify a nearby question where that knowledge does not justify high confidence.
activities.context: Well, although I do not suppose that either of us knows anything really beautiful and good, I am better off than he is,—for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know. In this latter particular, then, I seem to have slightly the advantage of him.
rubric: I name genuine knowledge or skill.
I identify a limit rather than dismissing the skill.
I explain what additional evidence the nearby question would require.
